name: Internet Basics
objectives: Without notes, explain what the internet and the web are and the two main ways a device connects, naming Wi-Fi and mobile data correctly and when Wi-Fi saves your phone plan's data

Given a network name and password, join a Wi-Fi network on your phone, tablet or computer and name what to avoid on public Wi-Fi, connected without help and with banking and private information named as things to avoid

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What the internet is
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain the internet, the web and how a device connects.
This lesson builds toward: Without notes, you will explain what the internet and the web are and the two main ways a device connects, naming Wi-Fi and mobile data correctly and when Wi-Fi saves your phone plan's data.
The internet is a huge network that links computers and phones all over the world so they can share information. The World Wide Web, or the web, is the part you visit with a web browser: websites with pages, pictures and videos. Email and video calls also travel over the internet.
Your device connects in one of two main ways. Wi-Fi is a wireless connection from a box called a router, at home, at a library or at a café. Mobile data comes from your phone company's cell towers and is part of your phone plan.
Wi-Fi at home usually does not use up your phone plan's data, so it is a good choice for videos and big downloads.
Words to know:
- Internet: a worldwide network that connects computers and phones.
- Web (World Wide Web): the websites you visit with a browser.
- Router: the box that sends out a Wi-Fi signal.
- Mobile data: internet from your phone company's cell towers, part of your phone plan.
Try it now: On your phone or tablet, look at the top of the screen. Find the Wi-Fi symbol (curved lines) or the mobile data symbol (bars or letters like 5G). Which one is on right now?
You can now explain what the internet and the web are, and tell whether your device is on Wi-Fi or mobile data.

options: A list of websites you saved
Internet from your phone company's cell towers, part of your phone plan
check.why: Mobile data comes from cell towers and is part of your phone plan.

check.q: You want to watch a long video on your phone at home. Which connection would you use?
options: Home Wi-Fi, so you do not use up your phone plan's data
Mobile data, because it is always free
No connection is needed for videos
check.why: Home Wi-Fi usually does not use up your phone plan's data.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Connecting to Wi-Fi
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Join a Wi-Fi network on a phone, tablet or computer.
This lesson builds toward: Given a network name and password, you will join a Wi-Fi network on your phone, tablet or computer and name what to avoid on public Wi-Fi, connected without help and with banking and private information named as things to avoid.
To join Wi-Fi, you need the network's name and its password. At home, both are often printed on a sticker on the router. At a library or café, ask staff or look for a sign.
On an iPhone or iPad: open Settings, tap Wi-Fi, tap the network name and type the password. On Android: open Settings, tap Network and internet or Connections, then Wi-Fi, choose the network and type the password. On a computer: click the Wi-Fi symbol near the clock, pick the network and type the password.
Public Wi-Fi is handy, but other people share it. On public Wi-Fi, avoid banking and do not type private information. Only join networks whose names you were given by staff, not ones with odd names.
Step by step:
- Find the network name and password (router sticker, staff or a sign).
- Open Settings, then Wi-Fi (on a computer, click the Wi-Fi symbol near the clock).
- Tap or click the network name.
- Type the password carefully; capital letters matter.
- Wait for the Wi-Fi symbol to appear at the top.
Words to know:
- Network name: the name a Wi-Fi connection shows in the list, also called the SSID.
- Wi-Fi password: the code you type to join a Wi-Fi network.
- Public Wi-Fi: Wi-Fi shared by many people in places like libraries and cafés.
Try it now: Open your Wi-Fi settings and find the list of networks. If you are at home or a library, join the right one. Check that the Wi-Fi symbol appears at the top.
You can now join a Wi-Fi network and use public Wi-Fi safely.

check.q: What two things do you need to join a Wi-Fi network?
options: The network's name and its password
A tab and a search engine
check.why: You choose the network by its name and type its password.

check.q: At a café, you see two networks: one the staff named and one called "FREE_FAST_WIFI_123". What would you do?
options: Join the odd one because it says free
Type your bank details to test the odd one
Join only the network the staff gave you
check.why: Only join networks whose names staff gave you, not ones with odd names.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Using a web browser
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Open a website by its address and move around with the back button and tabs.
This lesson builds toward: Using a web browser, you will open a website by typing its address, then use the back button, tabs and zoom, with the right site open, a second tab opened and the text made bigger.
A web browser is the app you use to visit websites. Common ones are Chrome, Safari, Edge and Firefox. At the top is the address bar, a long box where you type a web address like weather.gov and press Enter or Go.
Useful buttons: the back arrow returns to the page you were on; the circle arrow reloads the page. Tabs let you have several pages open at once, like folders on a desk. Open a new tab with the plus (+) button and switch by tapping or clicking a tab.
If words are too small, you can zoom. On a computer, hold Ctrl and press + (Command and + on a Mac); Ctrl and - makes it smaller. On a phone, spread two fingers apart on the screen.
Step by step:
- Open the browser (Chrome, Safari, Edge or Firefox).
- Tap the address bar at the top.
- Type a web address, such as weather.gov, and press Enter or Go.
- Use the back arrow to return.
- Press + to open a new tab.
- Zoom: Ctrl and + (Command and + on Mac), or spread two fingers on a phone.
Words to know:
- Web browser: the app you use to visit websites, like Chrome, Safari, Edge or Firefox.
- Address bar: the box at the top of the browser where you type a web address.
- Tab: one open page in the browser; you can have several open at once.
- Zoom: make what is on the screen bigger or smaller.
Try it now: Open a browser and type weather.gov in the address bar. Then open a new tab and go to your local library's website. Switch between the two tabs and make the text bigger on one of them.
You can now open websites by their address, use the back button, switch tabs and make text bigger.

check.q: What does the circle arrow in a browser do?
check.why: The circle arrow reloads the page you are on.

check.q: You are reading a recipe and want to check the weather without losing the recipe. What would you do?
options: Open a new tab with the plus (+) button
check.why: Tabs let you keep several pages open at once.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Finding things and staying safe

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Searching the web
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Search for something specific and open a useful result.
This lesson builds toward: Given something you need to find, you will search with a few key words and choose a useful result that is not an ad, reading the web address before opening the result.
If you do not know a web address, search for it. Type a few key words in the address bar or on a search site like Google or Bing, then press Enter. For example: "Springfield public library hours".
The results page shows a list of links. Each has a blue title, the web address in small print, and a short description. Read the web address before you tap. Results at the top marked "Sponsored" or "Ad" are paid ads.
You can also search with your voice. Tap the microphone in the search box and say what you want, such as "weather tomorrow".
Step by step:
- Tap the address bar or a search box.
- Type a few key words, such as the place, the town and what you want.
- Press Enter or the search button.
- Skip results marked Sponsored or Ad.
- Read the web address, then tap the result you want.
Words to know:
- Search: type words to find web pages about them.
- Results: the list of web pages the search finds.
- Link: words or a picture you tap to go to another page.
Try it now: Search for the opening hours of a place near you, such as a pharmacy or a park. Skip any ads, open the official result and find the hours.
You can now search the web and pick a useful, non-ad result.

check.q: On a results page, what does the small print under each blue title show?
check.why: Each result shows its web address in small print, so you can read it before you tap.

check.q: Your hands are busy and you want tomorrow's weather. What would you do?
options: Type a long story into the search box
Open a bookmark for a shopping site
Tap the microphone in the search box and say "weather tomorrow"
check.why: You can search with your voice by tapping the microphone.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Reading a web address and avoiding scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Tell a safe web address from a risky one and handle scary pop-ups.
This lesson builds toward: Given web addresses, a scary pop-up and a site you use often, you will tell a safe web address from a risky one, close fake pop-ups, and bookmark the official site to get back to it safely, choosing correctly every time and opening the saved site again with one tap.
A web address has a main part, the domain, just before the first single slash, such as irs.gov or amazon.com. That main part tells you who runs the site. Fake sites use look-alike names such as "amaz0n-deals.com" or "irs-refund.help".
Look for https and a lock symbol at the start of the address. It means the connection is private, but scammers can have it too, so the domain name still matters most.
Some fake pop-ups say your computer has a virus and give a phone number to call. The FTC says real security warnings will never ask you to call a phone number, and real tech companies will not call or text you about a problem. Do not call. Close the tab or browser; if it will not close, restart the device. If you are worried, ask someone you trust.
Step by step:
- Find the domain: the name just before the first single slash.
- Check that it is the real name you expected.
- Look for https and the lock, but do not trust them alone.
- Scary pop-up with a phone number? Do not call.
- Close the tab or restart the device.
- Report tech support scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Words to know:
- Domain: the main name in a web address that tells you who runs the site, like irs.gov.
- Pop-up: a small window that suddenly appears on top of a web page.
- Tech support scam: a fake warning or call that says your device has a problem to get your money or access.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to spot, avoid and report tech support scams
Try it now: Look at three web addresses on your screen or in your email. For each one, point to the domain and say who runs the site.
You can now read a web address to see who runs a site and deal safely with fake virus pop-ups.

check.q: Which part of a web address tells you who runs the site?
options: The words after the first single slash
The domain, just before the first single slash
check.why: The domain, such as irs.gov, tells you who runs the site.

check.q: A pop-up says your computer has a virus and shows a number to call. It will not close. What would you do?
options: Restart the device and do not call
Type your card number to pay for a fix
Leave it on the screen for days
check.why: Real security warnings never ask you to call; restart if the pop-up will not close.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Saving your favorite sites
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Bookmark a website and open it again with one tap.
This lesson builds toward: Given web addresses, a scary pop-up and a site you use often, you will tell a safe web address from a risky one, close fake pop-ups, and bookmark the official site to get back to it safely, choosing correctly every time and opening the saved site again with one tap.
A bookmark (also called a favorite) saves a website so you can come back without searching again. It is the safest way back to sites you use often, like your bank, pharmacy or a news site, because you skip fake search results.
On a computer, click the star at the end of the address bar. On an iPhone or iPad in Safari, tap the Share button and choose Add Bookmark. In Chrome on a phone, open the menu (three dots) and tap the star. On many phones you can also choose "Add to Home screen" to make an icon like an app.
To open a bookmark later, open the bookmarks list in the browser menu, or tap the icon on your home screen.
Step by step:
- Open the official website you want to save.
- Computer: click the star in the address bar.
- Safari on iPhone or iPad: Share button, then Add Bookmark.
- Chrome on a phone: three-dot menu, then the star.
- To open it later: go to Bookmarks in the menu, or tap the home screen icon.
Words to know:
- Bookmark / favorite: a saved link to a website so you can open it again quickly.
- Home screen: the main screen of a phone or tablet that shows app icons.
Try it now: Final task: plan an outing. Search for a park, museum or library, open its official site, check its hours and address, open tomorrow's weather in a second tab, make the text bigger if needed, and bookmark the official site.
You can now go online on your own, find what you need, avoid fake sites and save your favorite sites.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Connecting to Wi-Fi The device is not connected, or a network with an unknown name was joined. The device is connected to a known Wi-Fi network without help. Also explains what to avoid on public Wi-Fi. Finding the official site The site opened is an ad or not the place's own site. The place's official website is found by search, and its hours and address are found. The web address was read and checked before tapping. Using the browser Only one page was opened, or the learner could not get back to the first page. A second tab shows tomorrow's weather, and the learner switches between tabs. Also zooms the text to a comfortable size and uses the back button. Safe address and bookmark No bookmark, or a look-alike or ad site was bookmarked. The official site is bookmarked and opened again with one tap. Also explains how the domain shows the site is real. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: On a computer, what do you click to bookmark a website?
options: The star at the end of the address bar
check.why: The star at the end of the address bar saves a bookmark.

check.q: You order medicine from your pharmacy's website every month. How would you get back to it safely?
options: Search for it every time and tap the first ad
Bookmark the official site and open it from your bookmarks
Click a link from a text message
check.why: A bookmark from the official site skips fake search results.
